``` In prose, swap the element for the one HTML already has for this: ```tsx } /> ``` Every visual decision is a `--pui-separator-*` custom property, and the orientation is on `data-orientation`, so it can be re-skinned from plain CSS or targeted with Tailwind arbitrary variants (`data-[orientation=vertical]:...`) without wrapping.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: decorative
props.description:
Drops `role="separator"`, leaving the line visible but absent from the
accessibility tree.

Use it when the grouping is already conveyed some other way — a heading,
a landmark, a list — and the rule is only reinforcing it visually.
Announcing a boundary that the structure already communicates makes a
screen reader read the page's decoration out loud.

props.name: orientation
props.description:
Which way the rule runs — and therefore which axis it separates. A
`horizontal` rule is a line across the inline axis dividing stacked
content; a `vertical` one is a line down the block axis dividing content
in a row.

It is also what Base UI reports as `aria-orientation`, so it is a
semantic choice, not only a visual one.

props.name: variant
props.description:
The line style. A rule has exactly one visual dimension, so this is the
whole of it: `solid` for structural divisions, `dashed` or `dotted` for
softer, more provisional ones (a drop zone's edge, an optional section).

SliderRoot.name: SliderRoot
SliderRoot.description:
Groups every part of the slider and owns its value. Renders a `<div>` laid
out as a two-column grid: `Label` and `Value` share the first row, and
`Control` spans both columns underneath.

The generic is forwarded rather than widened, so a `number` value keeps
`onValueChange(value: number)` and an array keeps `readonly number[]` — the
distinction between a single-thumb and a range slider is carried entirely by
the shape of `value` / `defaultValue`.

```tsx
<Slider.Root defaultValue={40}>
  <Slider.Label>Volume</Slider.Label>
  <Slider.Value />
  <Slider.Control>
    <Slider.Track>
      <Slider.Indicator />
      <Slider.Thumb />
    </Slider.Track>
  </Slider.Control>
</Slider.Root>
```

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: ref
props.description: A ref to the root `<div>`.

props.name: size
props.description:
Size of the slider. Scales the track thickness, the thumb and the gap
between the rows together.

props.name: tone
props.description: Which semantic colour set the indicator and thumb draw from.

SliderLabel.name: SliderLabel
SliderLabel.description:
The slider's visible label. Renders a `<div>`, not a `<label>`, and is wired
to every thumb's hidden `<input>` with `aria-labelledby` — a native label
cannot point at more than one control, so a range slider would leave the
second thumb unnamed.

On a range slider this names the group; give each `Thumb` its own
`aria-label` ("Minimum price", "Maximum price") so the two are still
distinguishable.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

SliderValue.name: SliderValue
SliderValue.description:
The current value as text. Renders an `<output>`.

By default it prints the values formatted with `Slider.Root`'s `format` and
`locale`, joined with an en dash for a range. Pass a function as `children`
to compose your own — it receives the formatted strings and the raw numbers:

```tsx
<Slider.Value>{(formatted) => `${formatted[0]} to ${formatted[1]}`}</Slider.Value>
```

This is a visible duplicate of what `aria-valuetext` already announces, so
it is never the only way to read the value — but it is what makes a slider
usable for anyone who cannot judge a thumb's position by eye, which is why
every demo that has room for it renders one.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

SliderControl.name: SliderControl
SliderControl.description:
The interactive strip. Renders a `<div>` that is padded well beyond the
painted track, because *this* is the element that takes the pointer: a press
anywhere inside it moves the nearest thumb. The padding is what gives the
control its 24×24 minimum target (SC 2.5.8) without thickening the rail, and
`thumbAlignment="edge"` measures it, so changing the padding changes where
an edge-aligned thumb comes to rest.

Contains exactly one `Track`.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

SliderTrack.name: SliderTrack
SliderTrack.description:
The rail: the whole range from `min` to `max`. Renders a `<div>` that Base
UI gives `position: relative` inline, which is what the `Indicator` and the
`Thumb` are positioned against.

Its thickness must stay an explicit length rather than `auto` — Base UI sizes
the indicator's cross axis with `height: inherit` (`width: inherit` when
vertical), so an auto-sized track leaves the indicator with nothing to
inherit and it collapses.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

SliderIndicator.name: SliderIndicator
SliderIndicator.description:
The filled part of the rail. Renders a `<div>` inside `Track`.

Base UI owns its position and size through inline styles — `width` /
`height` for a single thumb, plus an offset from the start edge for a range
— so the stylesheet only paints it. Setting a width here would be
overwritten on the next render.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

SliderThumb.name: SliderThumb
SliderThumb.description:
One draggable handle. Renders a `<div>` wrapping a visually hidden
`<input type="range">` — the input is the real control, so it is what takes
focus and what a screen reader reads.

That split is why the focus ring is `.pui-focus-ring-within` rather than
`.pui-focus-ring`: the thumb `<div>` never matches `:focus-visible` itself.

A range slider needs one `Thumb` per value, each with an `index` — without
it the thumbs only find their order once the composite list has registered
on the client, so a server-rendered range slider paints both handles at the
first value and jumps on hydration. Give each one an `aria-label` too; the
`Label` names the group, not the individual handles.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

Spinner.name: Spinner
Spinner.description:
A busy indicator, in four flavours.

Base UI has no spinner primitive — there is no interaction to model and no
state machine to get right — so this is the one component in the library
that is not built on one. What it does have is the part everybody gets
wrong: an indicator that is announced once and correctly, and an animation
that stays informative when the user has asked for less motion.

```tsx
<Spinner />
<Spinner variant="bars" size="lg" label="Loading invoices" labelPlacement="end" />
<Spinner decorative variant="dots" tone="current" />
```

Styling is driven by `data-*` attributes and `--pui-spinner-*` custom
properties, so it can be re-skinned from plain CSS or targeted with Tailwind
arbitrary variants (`data-[variant=dots]:...`) without wrapping.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: decorative
props.description:
Stops the spinner announcing itself: no `role="status"`, and no hidden
label.

Use it whenever something else already announces the wait — a `Button`
with `loading`, a panel that sets `aria-busy`, a live region that swaps in
the loaded content. Two announcements for one wait is worse than one, and
a page that mounts six spinners with six live regions is unusable.

A label you asked to SHOW stays visible and stays in the accessibility
tree, as ordinary text. Text that is on screen but hidden from assistive
technology is a bug in its own right, so `decorative` will not do that —
it only ever removes the live region and the invisible label.

props.name: label
props.description:
What the spinner is waiting on. This is the only thing that reaches a
screen reader — the indicator itself is `aria-hidden`, because a picture
of motion is not information.

Say what is happening rather than that something is: "Loading invoices"
tells someone whether the wait concerns them; "Loading" does not.

props.name: labelPlacement
props.description:
Where the label goes. `hidden` keeps it in the accessibility tree but out
of the paint; `end` and `bottom` also show it, which is what you want for
a wait long enough that the user deserves to know what it is for.

props.name: size
props.description:
Diameter of the indicator — `1rem`, `1.5rem` or `2rem`. Every variant is
laid out as a fraction of it, so all four occupy exactly the same box and
can be swapped without moving anything around them.

props.name: tone
props.description:
Which semantic colour set the indicator draws from. `current` takes
`currentColor` instead, which is what makes a spinner dropped inside a
button or a link match the text beside it.

props.name: variant
props.description:
Which indicator to draw. All four are the same size and cost the same —
this is a question of voice, not of capability.

`ring` is a rotating comet, the neutral default. `dots` is three bouncing
dots, which reads as friendlier and suits inline text. `bars` is eight
fading spokes — the only variant whose animation is identical with and
without reduced motion, so it is the safest choice for something that must
look the same for everyone. `pulse` is a breathing halo, best for ambient
"still working" states rather than for blocking ones.

Switch.name: Switch

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s) for the track. Applied after the internal styles
so consumer utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: id
props.description:
The id of the hidden `<input>` element — or of the root element when
`nativeButton` is `true`. Point a sibling `<label htmlFor>` at whichever
of the two your `nativeButton` setting produces.

props.name: nativeButton
props.description:
Whether the rendered element is a native `<button>`. Base UI defaults
this to `false` here — the opposite of trigger-style parts — because the
root renders a `<span>` so that an enclosing `<label>` stays valid HTML.

Set it (together with `render={<button />}`) for the sibling-label
`htmlFor`/`id` pattern. Note that it also moves `id`: with `nativeButton`
the `id` lands on the root element, otherwise on the hidden input.

props.name: size
props.description:
Size of the switch. Track, thumb and travel distance all scale together,
so the thumb always lands flush against the end of the track.

props.name: stateIcon
props.description:
Draw a checkmark inside the thumb while the switch is on.

This is the switch's non-positional state cue, and it is why the default
is `true`: a user who cannot perceive the thumb sliding still gets a
glyph appearing. Turning it off leaves colour as the only cue that does
not depend on noticing movement.

props.name: thumbClassName
props.description: Additional class name(s) for the thumb, for the same reason.

TabsRoot.name: TabsRoot
TabsRoot.description:
Groups the tab strip and its panels.

Note the Base UI default: `defaultValue` is `0`, an *index*, not the first
tab's string value. With string values and no `defaultValue`, Base UI emits
an automatic `onValueChange` with reason `'initial'` to correct itself, so
always pass `defaultValue` (or `value`) pointing at an **enabled** tab —
during server rendering a disabled first tab is not skipped. `null` is a
legal "nothing active" value and is deliberately not normalised away.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: variant
props.description:
Which indicator treatment the tab strip uses. `"line"` draws a rail with a
sliding underline; `"pill"` draws a filled pill that slides behind the
active tab. Both are the same indicator element moved by the same CSS
variables — only the geometry differs.

TabsList.name: TabsList
TabsList.description:
The tab strip. Must contain the `Indicator`, which is positioned against
this element — the stylesheet gives it `position: relative` for exactly that
reason.

props.name: activateOnFocus
props.description:
Whether arrow-key focus also activates the tab it lands on. Left `false`
so arrow keys only move focus and activation happens on Enter or Space —
automatic activation loads every panel the user arrows past, which is
hostile when a panel fetches data.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: loopFocus
props.description: Whether arrow-key focus wraps from the last tab back to the first.

TabsTab.name: TabsTab

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

TabsIndicator.name: TabsIndicator
TabsIndicator.description:
The sliding marker. Base UI publishes the active tab's geometry on this
element as `--active-tab-left` / `--active-tab-top` / `--active-tab-width` /
`--active-tab-height` (already px values, consumed directly, never wrapped
in `calc()` as raw numbers) and the stylesheet turns those into a `translate`
+ size transition.

Renders inside `Tabs.List`, never outside it.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: renderBeforeHydration
props.description:
Whether to emit a tiny inline script that positions the indicator before
React hydrates. Defaults to `true` here rather than Base UI's `false`:
without it a server-rendered tab strip shows no indicator at all until
hydration finishes, which reads as a broken selection.

TabsPanel.name: TabsPanel
TabsPanel.description:
The content region for one tab. Base UI gives it `tabIndex={0}` so keyboard
users can reach the content directly after the strip — which is why it
carries the focus ring as well as the Tab does.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: keepMounted
props.description:
Whether the panel stays in the DOM while hidden. Required if you want the
exit transition to play, or if the panel holds scroll position or
uncommitted form state that should survive a round trip.

Toggle.name: Toggle
Toggle.description:
A two-state button that is either on or off, built on Base UI's unstyled
`Toggle` primitive. Renders a `<button>` with `aria-pressed`.

Reach for it when the button *is* the state — bold, mute, pin, favourite —
and the effect is immediate and local. If the state is a setting the user
confirms later, use [`Switch`](/components/switch) or
[`Checkbox`](/components/checkbox), which carry a label and a form value; a
toggle button has neither.

State is exposed on `data-*` attributes (`data-pressed`, `data-disabled`)
and every visual decision is a `--pui-toggle-*` custom property, so it can
be re-skinned from plain CSS or targeted with Tailwind arbitrary variants
(`data-[pressed]:...`) without wrapping.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: iconOnly
props.description:
Render as a square button sized for a single icon, holding the 24×24
minimum hit target from WCAG SC 2.5.8. Always pair with `aria-label` —
an icon is not an accessible name.

props.name: ref
props.description:
Ref to the button element. Declared as a prop rather than through
`forwardRef` because the component is generic — a `forwardRef` wrapper
would erase `Value` and with it the inference on `value`.

props.name: size
props.description:
Size of the button. Matches `Button` step for step so the two line up in
one toolbar. Inherited from an enclosing `ToggleGroup` when left unset.

props.name: tone
props.description:
Which semantic colour set the pressed state draws from. Combines freely
with `variant`. Inherited from an enclosing `ToggleGroup` when left unset.

props.name: value
props.description:
A unique string identifying this toggle within a `ToggleGroup`. Required
inside a group — the group's value is the list of pressed toggles' values,
so a toggle without one can never appear in it. Ignored outside a group,
where `pressed` / `defaultPressed` carry the state instead.

props.name: variant
props.description:
How loud the *pressed* state is. Unpressed is quiet in every variant —
that is what makes a toggle read as off — so the variant only decides what
"on" looks like: `solid` fills with the tone, `soft` tints with it,
`outline` tints and keeps a border that is also drawn while unpressed.

There is deliberately no `ghost`: every variant is already chromeless at
rest, so a ghost toggle would differ from `soft` in nothing but its
pressed fill — and dropping that fill would leave hue as the only cue
separating on from off.

Inherited from an enclosing `ToggleGroup` when left unset.

ToggleGroup.name: ToggleGroup
ToggleGroup.description:
Shared state for a series of `Toggle`s, built on Base UI's `ToggleGroup`
primitive. Renders a `<div role="group">`.

Like `RadioGroup` this is a keyboard mode as well as a state container: the
whole group is one tab stop and the arrow keys move between toggles. Unlike
a radio group, moving does **not** select — arrowing past a toggle leaves it
untouched, and Space or Enter is what presses it. That makes a toggle group
safe for choices a radio group is not, including ones that fire a request.

The group has no implicit accessible name. `role="group"` is not a labelable
element, so give it `aria-label` or point `aria-labelledby` at your own
heading.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The values pressed on mount when uncontrolled.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disable every toggle in the group.

props.name: fullWidth
props.description:
Stretch the group to fill its container and share the space equally
between the toggles. Mostly useful with `segmented`, where an evenly
divided strip is the expected shape.

props.name: multiple
props.description:
Allow several toggles to be pressed at once. With it off, pressing one
unpresses the rest — but pressing the pressed one still turns it off, so
"nothing selected" stays reachable in a way a radio group never allows.

props.name: orientation
props.description:
Direction the toggles are laid out in, and the axis the arrow keys move
along. Unlike `RadioGroup`'s, this is not layout-only: Base UI binds the
arrows to the named axis, so a vertical group answers to Up and Down and
leaves Left and Right to the page.

props.name: ref
props.description:
Ref to the group element. Declared as a prop rather than through
`forwardRef` because the component is generic — a `forwardRef` wrapper
would erase `Value` and with it the typing of `onValueChange`.

props.name: segmented
props.description:
Draw the group as a segmented control: one padded panel behind the whole
set, with the toggles closed up inside it. Off, the group is just a row of
separate buttons — right for a toolbar, where the toggles are neighbours
rather than alternatives.

Pair it with `variant="solid"` for the classic filled segmented control.

props.name: size
props.description:
Default `size` for every `Toggle` inside the group. A toggle's own `size`
still wins.

props.name: tone
props.description:
Default `tone` for every `Toggle` inside the group. A toggle's own `tone`
still wins.

props.name: value
props.description:
The values of every pressed toggle. Pairs with `onValueChange` for a
controlled group; use `defaultValue` for an uncontrolled one. Always an
array, including when `multiple` is false — it is then empty or holds one
value.

props.name: variant
props.description:
Default `variant` for every `Toggle` inside the group. A toggle's own
`variant` still wins.

TooltipProvider.name: TooltipProvider
TooltipProvider.description:
Shares one hover delay across every tooltip beneath it. Renders no DOM
element.

Mount it once near the root of the app. Without it each tooltip waits out
its own delay, so sweeping across a toolbar feels sticky.

props.name: children
props.description: The subtree that shares this delay.

props.name: closeDelay
props.description: How long to wait before closing a tooltip, in milliseconds.

props.name: delay
props.description:
How long to wait before opening a tooltip, in milliseconds. Applies to
every tooltip below this provider; an individual `Tooltip.Trigger` can
still override it.

props.name: timeout
props.description:
Grouping window, in milliseconds. If one tooltip closes and another opens
within this window, the second one appears instantly instead of waiting
out `delay` again — which is what makes a row of icon buttons feel like a
single toolbar rather than a series of separate waits.

TooltipRoot.name: TooltipRoot
TooltipRoot.description:
Groups one tooltip's trigger and popup. Renders no DOM element, so it takes
no `className`, `style` or `ref`.

props.name: actionsRef
props.description:
Imperative escape hatch. `unmount()` forces the popup out of the DOM (use
it when an exit animation is driven externally); `close()` closes the
tooltip.

props.name: children
props.description:
The trigger and popup for this tooltip. May also be a render function
receiving `{ payload }` from the trigger that opened the tooltip.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description:
Whether the tooltip is open when it first mounts. For a controlled
tooltip use `open` instead.

props.name: defaultTriggerId
props.description:
The initially attached trigger id. Pairs with `defaultOpen` the way
`triggerId` pairs with `open`.

props.name: disabled
props.description:
Whether this tooltip is disabled. Disables the tooltip only — the trigger
element stays fully interactive and does not receive the `disabled`
attribute.

props.name: disableHoverablePopup
props.description:
Whether the popup can be hovered without closing. Off by default: a
tooltip is not meant to hold interactive content, and a hoverable popup
gets in the way of the content beneath it.

props.name: handle
props.description:
Associates this tooltip with detached triggers created through
`Tooltip.createHandle()`, so one popup can serve several triggers that
live elsewhere in the tree.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description:
Called when the tooltip wants to open or close. The second argument
carries the reason (`'trigger-hover'`, `'trigger-focus'`,
`'trigger-press'`, `'outside-press'`, `'escape-key'`, `'disabled'`,
`'imperative-action'`, `'none'`) and can `cancel()` the change.

props.name: onOpenChangeComplete
props.description:
Called after the open or close transition has finished. Use this rather
than a timer when work has to wait for the popup to actually leave.

props.name: open
props.description:
Whether the tooltip is currently open. Pass this together with
`onOpenChange` to control the tooltip.

props.name: trackCursorAxis
props.description:
Which axis the tooltip follows the cursor on. `'both'` turns it into a
cursor-tracking label; combine with `side="bottom"` for the usual feel.

props.name: triggerId
props.description:
The trigger the tooltip is attached to, for controlled multi-trigger
setups. There is no separate `onTriggerIdChange` — derive the new id from
`eventDetails.trigger` inside `onOpenChange`.

TooltipTrigger.name: TooltipTrigger
TooltipTrigger.description:
The element the tooltip is attached to. Renders a `<button>`.

**This trigger must carry its own accessible name.** The tooltip is a
visual affordance only — see the note on {@link Tooltip} — so an icon-only
trigger needs an `aria-label` that closely matches the tooltip's text.
Screen reader users get the `aria-label` and nothing else.

Unlike `Popover.Trigger` and `Menu.Trigger`, this part has **no
`nativeButton` prop**; it always renders button semantics. Compose it with
an existing control through `render` instead.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: closeDelay
props.description: How long to wait before closing, in milliseconds.

props.name: closeOnClick
props.description:
Whether clicking the trigger closes the tooltip. Leave it on for triggers
that do something on click — the tooltip has served its purpose by then
and would otherwise sit over the result.

props.name: delay
props.description:
How long to wait before opening, in milliseconds. Overrides the
provider's `delay` for this trigger only.

props.name: disabled
props.description:
Stops this trigger from opening the tooltip. It does **not** apply the
`disabled` attribute to the element, so the button stays focusable and
clickable; style the difference from `data-trigger-disabled`. To disable
the control itself, pass `disabled` through `render`.

props.name: handle
props.description:
Associates a detached trigger with a `Tooltip.Root` that carries the same
handle, created once outside render with `Tooltip.createHandle()`.

props.name: payload
props.description:
Data handed to the tooltip when this trigger opens it, so one popup can
render different content per trigger.

props.name: ref
props.description: Forwarded to the underlying element.

props.name: render
props.description:
Replaces the rendered `<button>` with another element or component —
`render={<Button variant="ghost" />}` is the common case. Note there is
no `nativeButton` prop on this part: it always renders button semantics.

TooltipPopup.name: TooltipPopup
TooltipPopup.description:
The tooltip surface. Renders the portal, the positioner and the popup in
one part, so the common case is a single element in consumer markup.

Keep the content to a short visual label. Anything a user must read to
operate the UI belongs in the page or in a `Popover` — see {@link Tooltip}.

props.name: align
props.description: How the tooltip lines up with the trigger along the chosen side.

props.name: alignOffset
props.description:
Shifts the tooltip along the alignment axis, in pixels, or a function
returning one.

props.name: anchor
props.type: Element | VirtualElement | RefObject<Element | null> | (() => Element | VirtualElement | null) | null
props.description:
The element the tooltip positions against, when it should not be the
trigger.

props.name: arrowPadding
props.description:
Minimum distance, in pixels, the arrow keeps from the tooltip's corners
before it is allowed to sit off-centre (`data-uncentered`).

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.

props.name: collisionAvoidance
props.description:
How the tooltip reacts when it would overflow the boundary — whether it
flips, shifts, or stays put.

props.name: collisionBoundary
props.description: The boundary the tooltip tries to stay inside of.

props.name: collisionPadding
props.description: Space, in pixels, kept between the tooltip and the collision boundary.

props.name: container
props.type: HTMLElement | ShadowRoot | RefObject<HTMLElement | ShadowRoot | null> | null
props.description:
Where the portal renders. Defaults to `document.body`; point it at a
container when the tooltip has to live inside a specific stacking or
shadow root.

props.name: disableAnchorTracking
props.description:
Stops the tooltip re-measuring the anchor on scroll and resize. Cheaper,
but the tooltip drifts if the anchor moves.

props.name: keepMounted
props.description: Keeps the portal in the DOM while the tooltip is closed.

props.name: positionerClassName
props.description:
Additional class name(s) for the positioner element, which owns
placement and `z-index`. Use it to re-stack a single tooltip.

props.name: positionMethod
props.description:
Whether the tooltip is positioned with `position: absolute` or
`position: fixed`.

props.name: side
props.description:
Which side of the trigger to place the tooltip on. Flips automatically to
avoid collisions. `"inline-start"` / `"inline-end"` follow writing
direction.

props.name: sideOffset
props.description:
Gap between trigger and tooltip, in pixels, or a function returning one.
When an `Arrow` is rendered this must exceed the arrow's height or the
arrow will overlap the trigger; the default leaves room for the default
arrow.

props.name: sticky
props.description:
Keeps the tooltip glued to the trigger while it scrolls out of view
instead of letting it detach.

TooltipArrow.name: TooltipArrow
TooltipArrow.description:
The wedge pointing back at the trigger. Render it as the first child of
`Tooltip.Popup`.

It is an SVG rather than the traditional CSS-border triangle on purpose: in
forced-colors mode every border colour is forced to `CanvasText`, and a
border triangle degrades into a filled rectangle. Two flat paths cannot
fail that way.

props.name: children
props.description:
Replaces the built-in wedge. The default SVG inherits the popup's colours
through `--pui-tooltip-bg`, so a custom skin usually needs nothing here.

props.name: className
props.description:
Additional class name(s). Applied after the internal styles so consumer
utilities (e.g. Tailwind) win without needing `!important`.
